common_name: Nam Doc Mai Mango (Thai Honey Mango)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring once frost danger has fully passed, in a full-sun site with sharp drainage; the moderate, semi-compact growth habit takes well to large-container culture where winters occasionally threaten zone 9b.

directions: This classic Thai cultivar produces slender, curved fruit with thin golden-yellow skin blushed pink and exceptionally sweet, fiberless, low-acid flesh once ripe, though it is also prized green for eating with sticky rice or salt-chili dip while still tart and crisp. Its comparatively moderate vigor and manageable size make it one of the better mango cultivars for containers and small yards. Humid climates favor anthracnose on flowers and young fruit, so maintain an open canopy through annual pruning and consider a copper fungicide program through bloom.

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after all frost risk has passed; give this vigorous, upright cultivar generous room to reach full size, and stake young trees against wind until well established.

directions: Bred in Delray Beach, Florida, this cultivar bears very large, elongated fruit with orange-yellow skin blushed red and rich, fiberless, sweet flesh with a relatively small seed. It shows notably better field tolerance to anthracnose than many older cultivars, making it a dependable choice for humid Gulf Coast summers. Fruit typically ripens early to midsummer; harvest when the shoulders swell and a few fruits begin to color, then allow the rest of the crop to finish ripening at room temperature indoors.

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after frost danger passes, in a large, open, well-drained site; Choquette is a Type B bloomer, so plant near a Type A cultivar such as Simmonds or Winter Mexican for heavier fruit set.

directions: A West Indian x Guatemalan hybrid bred in Florida, Choquette is known for producing some of the largest avocados grown in home gardens, with individual fruit often exceeding three pounds. The thin, glossy green skin encloses mild, buttery, relatively low-oil flesh typical of West Indian-influenced cultivars. Its late harvest window, generally October through December, extends the backyard avocado season well past most other Florida cultivars, but the tree's ultimate size calls for a spacious planting site away from structures.

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun with excellent drainage; as a Type A bloomer it will set some fruit alone, but pairing with a Type B cultivar improves yields. Its Mexican-race cold hardiness makes it one of the better avocados to try in protected zone 9 sites.

directions: This Mexican-race avocado is grown less for fruit size than for cold hardiness, tolerating brief drops into the low-to-mid 20s Fahrenheit once established, which puts it within reach of gardeners at the cooler northern edge of avocado country. Fruit is small, six to ten ounces, with thin, dark purple-black skin and rich, high-oil flesh carrying the anise-scented foliage and fruit typical of Mexican-race types. Harvest runs fall into early winter; because the tree tends toward biennial bearing, thinning a heavy crop can help even out production year to year.

common_name: Hak Ip Lychee (Haak Yip, Black Leaf Lychee)

planting.note: Plant a grafted or air-layered tree in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil sheltered from wind; in zones 10-11 fall planting after summer heat breaks is preferred, while zone 9 sites should choose the warmest microclimate available.

directions: Named for its dark, glossy foliage, this mid-season Chinese cultivar is valued for consistent bearing in humid subtropical climates where many other lychee cultivars fruit erratically. The medium-size fruit has thin, bumpy, rose-red skin over sweet, aromatic, juicy flesh wrapped around a small seed. Like other lychees it needs several weeks of cool, dry nights in winter to set flower buds, so withhold irrigation during that stretch rather than watering on a fixed schedule; ripening falls in late spring to early summer and fruit should be picked promptly, as birds and squirrels find it just as appealing as people do.

common_name: Gros Michel Banana (Big Mike, Original Commercial Banana)

planting.note: Plant a rooted division (pup) after the last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; give this tall cultivar wind protection and ample room, since the pseudostem can exceed fifteen feet.

directions: Gros Michel was the dominant export banana worldwide until Fusarium wilt (Panama disease) devastated commercial plantations by the mid-twentieth century, prompting the industry-wide switch to Cavendish types. Home gardeners still seek it out for its richer, more intensely banana-flavored fruit and thicker, sturdier peel compared to modern supermarket bananas. The tall, vigorous pseudostem needs a wind-sheltered spot and heavy irrigation and feeding through the growing season; avoid planting in soil where bananas have previously declined, since the Fusarium pathogen persists indefinitely once established.

planting.note: Plant a container-grown tree in spring after frost risk passes, in full sun with well-drained soil; protect young trees their first two winters, since the root system is hardier than the topgrowth.

directions: A favorite fresh-eating guava across South Texas and Florida dooryards, this cultivar bears thin yellow skin over creamy white, very sweet, low-acid flesh with comparatively few seeds. It fruits on new wood, so an annual late-winter prune keeps the shrub-form tree compact and stimulates a fresh flush of fruiting growth. Roots generally survive brief dips to around 28°F even when the canopy freezes back, so zone 9 gardeners should mulch heavily and expect to regrow top growth after a hard freeze; in warm years the plant can produce two overlapping harvests.

planting.note: Plant a rooted cutting in spring after all frost danger has passed, next to a sturdy post or trellis for the climbing stems to grip; in zone 9 grow in a large container that can be sheltered during cold snaps.

directions: A white-fleshed dragon fruit selection favored by growers for reliable self-fertility and good yields without hand-pollination between different plants, though hand-pollinating night-blooming flowers still improves fruit set and size. Fruit is medium to large with red-pink scaled skin and sweet, mildly floral white flesh studded with tiny black seeds. As an epiphytic cactus it needs gritty, fast-draining soil and infrequent deep watering rather than a regular irrigation schedule, plus excellent air circulation to avoid stem rot. Provide a stout post or trellis at planting, since the three-ribbed stems climb by aerial roots and become heavy as the plant matures.
